title: Roadmap 05: DSA foundations
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: The interview routine plus the core patterns: hashing and prefix sums, sliding window, monotonic stack, binary search (including on the answer), linked lists and binary trees.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: In a coding interview, what should you do right after hearing the problem and before writing any code?

options.text: Restate it, clarify edge cases, then propose a brute force.
options.why: Right: this shows the routine and avoids solving the wrong problem.

options.text: Start coding the fastest-looking solution you can remember right away.
options.why: Coding first risks answering a different question than the one asked.

options.text: Stay silent while you privately work out the best possible answer first.
options.why: Silence hides your reasoning; interviewers grade the thinking too.

options.text: Write the final test suite first and skip any talk about the approach.
options.why: Tests matter, but they come after the approach is agreed.

questions.explanation: A solid routine is clarify, brute force, better idea, code, dry run, test cases, complexity. Saying the brute force first gives you a correct baseline and a hook for the optimisation.

questions.prompt: Count the subarrays of an integer array (negative numbers allowed) whose sum equals k. Select all statements that are true.

options.text: Keeping a running prefix sum and a map of prefix-sum counts solves it in O(n) time.
options.why: Right: for each index you add count[prefix - k] to the answer.

options.text: The map must start with {0: 1} so subarrays that begin at index 0 are counted.
options.why: Right: an empty prefix has sum 0 and must be countable.

options.text: A two-pointer sliding window is also correct, because the sum only grows as the window widens.
options.why: With negative numbers widening can lower the sum, so the window logic breaks.

options.text: Store only the first index of each prefix sum so every matching subarray is counted.
options.why: First-index storage suits longest-subarray problems; counting needs frequencies.

questions.explanation: Prefix sums turn "sum of a range" into a subtraction, and a hash map finds earlier prefixes in O(1). Sliding window needs non-negative values (a monotone sum).

options.text: O(n^2): the window is re-scanned from left for every new r.
options.why: There is no inner loop; left jumps directly using the dictionary.

options.text: O(n): r advances once and left never moves backwards.
options.why: Right: each index is visited once and dict operations are O(1) on average.

options.text: O(n log n): dictionary lookups cost log n on every iteration.
options.why: Python dict lookups are O(1) on average, not logarithmic.

options.text: O(n * k): seen is rebuilt for each of the k distinct letters.
options.why: seen is never rebuilt; it is only updated one key per step.

questions.explanation: Both pointers only move forward, so the work is linear (average case for the hash map). Reasoning about pointer movement is how you justify sliding window complexity.

questions.prompt: True or false: a monotonic stack solution for "next greater element" is O(n^2) because the while loop inside the for loop can pop many items for a single element.

options.text: True
options.why: The nested loop looks quadratic, but the pops are bounded in total.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total is O(n).

questions.explanation: Amortised analysis: count total pushes and pops across the whole run, not per iteration. Use a monotonic stack for next greater/smaller element, daily temperatures and histogram problems.

options.text: lo = mid + 1 should be lo = mid, otherwise some elements are skipped.
options.why: lo = mid can loop forever when hi = lo + 1; mid + 1 is correct here.

options.text: The loop must use lo <= hi, or the last remaining candidate is never checked.
options.why: Right: for a = [5] and t = 5, the loop never runs and -1 is returned.

options.text: mid must be (lo + hi) / 2, because the subtraction form gives a wrong index.
options.why: lo + (hi - lo) / 2 is the overflow-safe form and is correct.

options.text: hi should start at a.length rather than a.length - 1 to include the last index.
options.why: With hi = mid - 1 an inclusive hi is right; a.length - 1 is correct.

questions.explanation: Pick one invariant and keep it consistent: with an inclusive [lo, hi] range, loop while lo <= hi and move with mid + 1 and mid - 1. Dry run a one-element array to catch this.

questions.prompt: True or false: binary searching on the answer, for example the smallest ship capacity that delivers all packages within D days, is valid because feasibility is monotonic (once a capacity works, every larger one works too).

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: a monotonic yes/no predicate is what lets you discard half the range.

options.text: False
options.why: This is the real condition; without monotonicity the halving step is unsafe.

questions.explanation: Define a feasible(x) check, find the search range (lowest and highest possible answer), then binary search for the first x where feasible is true. Complexity is O(check cost * log range).

questions.prompt:
This Python function is meant to reverse a singly linked list. For the list 1 -> 2 -> 3, what does it return?

def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = cur.next
    return prev

options.text: 3 -> 2 -> 1: the list is reversed correctly in place.
options.why: cur.next is overwritten before it is saved, so the walk breaks.

options.text: None: the loop body is skipped and prev is never set.
options.why: The loop runs once because head is not None.

options.text: Node 1 only, with next None: the list is cut short.
options.why: Right: cur.next became None, so cur = cur.next ends the loop after one step.

options.text: It never terminates: the pointers form a cycle in the list.
options.why: The single relink points node 1 to None, so no cycle appears.

questions.explanation: Save the next node first (nxt = cur.next), then relink, then advance prev and cur. Losing the pointer before saving it is the classic reversal bug; always dry run on three nodes.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about binary trees that are true.

options.text: Validating a BST by passing (low, high) bounds down the recursion catches a deep node that breaks an ancestor's range.
options.why: Right: comparing only with the parent would miss that case.

options.text: An in-order traversal of a valid BST with distinct keys visits values in strictly increasing order.
options.why: Right: left subtree, node, right subtree gives sorted order.

options.text: It is enough to check that every node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
options.why: A node deep in the left subtree can still be larger than the root.

options.text: A preorder traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted order.
options.why: Preorder visits the node first, so the root comes before smaller left values.

options.text: The lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a general binary tree can be found recursively in O(n) time.
options.why: Right: return the node when both sides report a hit or the node is p or q.

questions.explanation: Know the three traversals and what each is good for. Serialisation usually uses preorder with null markers (or level order) so the tree can be rebuilt unambiguously.
